game:item-handbooktext-boat-sailed-*:
Sailboats are constructed in place on land, and then rolled into the water. They cannot be picked up. They can be deconstructed by holding down rightmouse with a saw. See the Building A Sailboat entry for more information.

Movement
Once you have constructed your sailboat, rightmouse click on the starboard aft seat (by the tiller at the stern) to sit in that seat: only that seat can control the boat. With the sails furled, you can use normal navigation keys to move the boat slowly. rightmouse-click on the cleat on the side of the mast (where a rope is tied) to unfurl the sail and pick up speed. The sailboat currently does not respond to wind direction, only your movement keys.

If the boat becomes grounded or in water that is too shallow, it can be moved very slowly using the arrow keys, but only with the sail furled again.

Equipping
Most boat accessories are added to the boat via ctrl + rightmouse.
The boat can also hold several passengers - in every boat, one passenger can sit on the port-side aft seat (adjacent to the player who is at the tiller controlling the boat). Additional seats can be added to any of the eight cargo hold spots.

You can place containers (including chests, baskets, and storage vessels) in the hold of the boat, and access them on or off the boat.

You can also place a mount (such as an elk) on the boat by first placing a wooden fence post in one of the cargo spots - being sure to leave 2 cargo spots empty aft of the post - and then using a rope on this fence post, which will place the animal into the aft cargo spots. You can then disembark the animal using rightmouse on the fence post.

You can attach a lantern to the aft face of the mast (about 3 meters up) to provide light.

Ratlines can be attached to the gunwhales on each side of the mast in order to allow you to climb to the top of the mast to look around.

An anchor can be placed in the front-left space in the prow. With an empty hand, rightmouse click it to let it go or haul it up; see Mooring and Anchoring.

There is also a spot at the prow for a figurehead to be placed (you can also place your own chiseled figurehead there), and on the port bow, your boat can be named (using pigment and shift + rightmouse-click).
game:item-handbooktext-anchor-stone: The stone anchor can be placed in the front-left prow location of the sailboat (and only this spot). With an empty hand, rightmouse click it to let it go or haul it up. It holds when about five times the depth of the water in rope is let out; see Mooring and Anchoring.

itemdesc-anchorwarp: Nine ropes spliced into 90 metres of warp. Stowed at a sailboat's mast, it lets the anchor reach deeper water.
itemdesc-bark-*: Peeled from a log with a knife. Patches a bark canoe on the way.
itemdesc-lath-*: Split from a pole with an axe, as long as the pole. Soaked in a barrel of water, it bends into a vessel's frame.

itemdesc-tholeoar-*: A three-metre oar with the bull that rides a currach's thole pin.
blockdesc-wedge-*: Set on a lying log. Each blow of an axe's butt drives it a step deeper. With one driven home in each log of a row of two to five end to end, the trunk splits into poles as long as the row.
handbook-createdby-pole: Split along the grain from two to five logs of one wood lying end to end, with a splitting wedge driven home in each by an axe
blockdesc-reedbundle-*: Reeds bound tight with rope, three metres long. Laid two side by side and bound with rope, they make a reed boat.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:re:
A float of two reed bundles, quick to bind and light to carry. It carries one person, sitting low and half in the water, and a basket.
Its bundles give under a knock on rock or a breaker and take no harm.
Reed soaks up water, and the ends sag as it soaks. After a day afloat the rider sits awash, and within four days the boat lies on the bottom.
Dry it ashore in the sun between trips. Each drying leaves it a little more rotten, and it can't be mended.

Building it
- Bind two reed bundles in the crafting grid, each from 144 cattail tops, papyrus tops or thatch and two ropes, with a knife.
- Hold a bundle and rightmouse the ground anywhere: it lies along the way you look.
- Hold the second bundle and rightmouse the first: it lies beside the first.
- Hold a rope on the pair. The first lashing binds them into the boat where they lie. From then on it floats and can be carried.
- Hold a second rope on the boat to lash it along its length.
- Hold a rope on each end to bind it up. With both ends bound up, the boat is finished.

Using it
- Paddle it with a paddle in hand, or pole it through shallows with a pole.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:du:
One log hollowed out: the toughest hull before planks. Rocks barely scratch it, and it needs no upkeep.
It is too heavy to carry: a workhorse of rivers and lakes.
In a sea it rolls hard and ships water over its low sides. Bail it with a bowl, jug or bucket before it swamps.

Building it
You burn and hew a dugout out of one trunk beside the water it will float on, because it is too heavy to carry there.
- Lay five logs of one wood on their sides, end to end along the shore, with water in the very next blocks.
- Hold an axe and shift + rightmouse the middle log. The logs become one trunk to work, where they lie.
- Hold rightmouse on the trunk with the axe to strip the bark, one side of a log at each stroke. Strip it all, because the fire burns on bare wood.
- Hold wet clay and rightmouse the trunk, a ball at a time, until clay runs along both edges and over both ends: 19 balls on the fresh trunk, fewer each fire as the hull narrows. The clay keeps the fire to the hollow. A fire lit without it chars the rim through and spoils the trunk.
- Lay dry grass on the trunk, then four firewood on the grass.
- Hold a torch or a firestarter and hold rightmouse on the trunk until it catches. A firestarter often fails, so hold it again. The grass catches first, then the wood.
- The fire smoulders for about a day and a half. Rain or water in the hollow puts it out: bail it and light it again. The fire burns whoever stands in it, as a campfire does.
- Once the fire is out, hold rightmouse on the trunk with the axe to hew out the char. The hewing takes the dried clay off with the rim, and shapes a sixth of the outside each time: the round bottom, the ends.
- Lay clay, dry grass and four firewood again, light the fire and hew. Six fires hollow it out.
- Walk into it from the shore to push it into the water. It floats at every stage, and an axe breaks it up at every stage, but it gets its seats only when finished.

Using it
- Sit in the front seat and paddle it with a paddle in hand, or pole it through shallows with a pole. The back seat carries a passenger.
- Mend it with a log of its own wood.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:co:
A bowl of hide on a basket of laths, for one person. It spins on the spot and goes poorly in a straight line: use it for fishing and short crossings.
It is light enough to carry on your back.

Building it
You begin a coracle as a pile of laths on the ground.
- Soak fourteen two-metre laths and three five-metre ones in a barrel of water.
- Hold a wet short lath and shift + rightmouse the ground to start a pile, then the pile to add the other thirteen. Fourteen short laths make one layer, and it lies as the lattice: seven along, seven across.
- A fifteenth lath starts a second layer, and no coracle comes of that pile.
- Hold a rope on the pile to bind the crossings. The first rope ties the lattice into the coracle where it lies.
- Hold the long laths on it to plait them round as the gunwale. They bend the lattice up into a bowl. Two days later the laths have dried and set.
- Hold hides on it to sew them on: any hide before it is leather. A small hide covers one part, a medium two, a large three, a huge five. The coracle takes two parts.
- Hold a rope on it to lace the cover to the gunwale, then grease the cover with rendered fat.

Using it
- Scull it over the bow with a paddle in hand, or pole it through shallows with a pole.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse, and put it in a backpack slot to carry it on your back.
- Grease it with rendered fat to stop its seams seeping. Mend holes in the hide with a small prepared hide.
- Untanned hide rots afloat within days in warm water, slower in cold. Dry the coracle ashore in the sun to keep it. Prepared hide lasts for years.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:ba:
Bark on a light frame. It is fast, and draws so little water that it runs rapids that batter every other hull but the coracle.
It is fragile, and light enough to carry over portages.

Building it
You build a bark canoe where its bark comes off the tree.
- Hold a knife and rightmouse a standing birch, elm or spruce whose trunk is at least five blocks tall. The bark comes off in one sheet and falls to the ground: the canoe, not yet framed. It floats and can be carried from the start.
- Split laths: lay five logs of one wood on their sides, end to end, set a splitting wedge on each, and drive the wedges with an axe.
- Soak the laths in a barrel of water for two days, because only wet laths bend.
- Hold the laths on the sheet one at a time. Lay the inner gunwales and the thwarts flat on the bark. The last thwart turns the middle of the bark up around them.
- Hold a knife on the canoe to slash the bark where it narrows. Each slash lets the next length turn up.
- Lay the first outer gunwale to raise the frame to full height, then lay the second.
- Hold the knife on the canoe again to trim each end, then lay the stems.
- Hold a rope on the canoe to lash the bark to the gunwales, then lay the sheathing and the ribs.
- Hold hot pitch glue on the canoe to pitch the seams, in a bowl, jug, bucket or the pot you cooked it in.
- Two days later the ribs have dried, and the canoe is finished and takes its seats.

Using it
- Sit in the back seat and paddle it with a paddle in hand, or pole it through shallows with a pole. The front seat carries a passenger.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse.
- Mend it on the way with bark of the same tree.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:la:
Hold an axe and split a pole in the crafting grid into 16 laths as long as the pole.
- Soak the laths in a barrel of water for two days, because only wet laths bend. Out of the water they dry again in two days.
- Hold a wet lath on a vessel being built to lay it in its place. Each piece takes any lath at least as long as it, cut down to size.
- Hold a lath and shift + rightmouse the ground to lay it in a pile, wet or dry. A pile of fourteen wet two-metre laths, or of two wet five-metre ones, bound with rope, starts a coracle or a currach.
- Only dry laths burn.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:po:
A row of logs splits into 64 poles as long as the row.
- Hold an axe and split a pole in the crafting grid into 16 laths.
- Hold a pole across a finished dugout to rig it into an outrigger. The booms, mast and spars take three-metre poles.
- Hold a pole on a vessel being built to set it in its place.
- Hold a pole in the seat that steers to pole the boat through shallows. You stand up to pole wherever the boat bears you, and sit where it is too narrow.
- A pole pushes off the bottom where the water is about a metre shallower than the pole is long, and finds nothing deeper.
- Stow a pole aboard with ctrl + rightmouse on the vessel.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:pa:
Carve a paddle from a two-metre pole with an axe and a knife in the crafting grid.
- Sit in a boat with the paddle in hand to paddle it: walkforward and walkbackward drive the boat, walkleft and walkright turn it. A paddle works in water of any depth.
- A paddle works on one side and turns the boat away from that side. To hold the course, you change sides on your own as the bow veers off, losing a stroke each time. To turn, you paddle on the side that turns the boat.
- Scull a coracle with a paddle over its bow.
- A paddle serves every boat but the currach, which you row with its own oars.
- Stow a paddle aboard with ctrl + rightmouse on the vessel.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:th:
Make a thole oar from a three-metre pole and a two-metre lath for its bull, with an axe and a knife in the crafting grid.
- A currach takes two, one on each thole pin, as the last step of its build. Hold an oar and rightmouse the currach to ship it.
- The oars stay aboard. Row the currach from the thwart with an empty hand.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:cu:
Greased hide on a frame of laths. It is light and carries cargo along the coast under oars.
Rocks hole the hide, and the seams seep unless you grease them with rendered fat every few days afloat.
The light hull flexes with the sea and rides over swells that come aboard heavier boats.

Building it
You build a currach upside down, its gunwale on the ground.
- Soak two five-metre laths in a barrel of water, and as many more as the frame takes: two- and three-metre ones for the ribs, five-metre ones for the stringers.
- Hold a wet long lath and shift + rightmouse the ground to start a pile, then the pile to add the second. The two must lie alone in the pile.
- Hold a rope on the pile to bind their ends. The first rope draws them together at the bow where they lie, and the second at the stern, closing the gunwale.
- Hold the ribs on it to bend them over the gunwale, then lay the stringers along them. Two days later the ribs have dried and set.
- Hold hides on it to sew them on: any hide before it is leather. A small hide covers one part, a medium two, a large three, a huge five. The currach takes eight parts.
- Hold a rope on it to lace the cover to the gunwale.
- Hold a two-metre pole on it to set it across as a thwart.
- Hold a thole oar on it to ship it on a thole pin, and a second one for the other pin.
- With an empty hand, rightmouse click the currach to turn it over, then grease the hide with rendered fat.

Using it
- Sit on the thwart and row it with an empty hand, or pole it through shallows with a pole in hand.
- Its bottom carries three baskets, storage vessels or chests: two forward of the rower and one aft of the rower's feet. Hold one and ctrl + rightmouse the currach to put it in its place.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse.
- Grease it with rendered fat to stop its seams seeping. Mend holes in the hide with a large prepared hide.
- Untanned hide rots afloat within days in warm water, slower in cold. Dry the currach ashore in the sun to keep it. Prepared hide lasts for years.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:ou:
A dugout steadied by a float on booms, under a crab-claw sail: the fastest thing at sea before metal.
It carries little cargo, is clumsy in tight water and is too heavy to carry.
The float keeps it very steady in a sea, but its low sides ship water as a dugout's do. Bail it with a bowl, jug or bucket, or sew on washstrakes to take it to sea.

Building it
You rig an outrigger from a finished dugout, where it lies.
- Split poles: lay three logs of one wood on their sides, end to end, set a splitting wedge on each, and drive the wedges with an axe.
- Lay three more logs of one wood on their sides along the dugout, a block off, the middle one beside the dugout's middle. They will be the float.
- Hold a pole across the dugout and rightmouse. The first boom joins the logs to the dugout: they become the float where they lie, still three logs, and the dugout becomes the outrigger, its hull as it was.
- Hold the other two booms on it. They rest on the gunwales and on the logs.
- Hold an axe on the float to hew it down, six passes all round. The booms settle onto it as it shrinks, until it is a round log with pointed ends.
- Hold a rope on it to lash the booms to the gunwales and to the float.
- Hold poles on it to set up the mast and the crab claw's two spars. Hold four pieces of linen cloth on it to bend on the sail, and rope to set up the stays and the sheet.
- Walk into it from the shore to push it into the water. It gets its seats only when finished.
- Any time after, once you have a saw, hold 12 planks on it: the washstrakes along its sides, end to end, and a board across each end. Then hold 5 ropes on it to sew them on. They raise its sides 15 cm for the open sea.

Using it
- Sit in the front seat and paddle and steer it with a paddle in hand, under sail too, or pole it through shallows with a pole. The back seat carries a passenger.
- rightmouse click the halyard cleat at the mast to raise or lower the sail.
- Mend it with a log of its own wood.
- Bind up the float's lashings with flax twine. Knocks on the float's side work them loose, and once they give out the float and the rig come away and leave a plain dugout.
guide-goingtosea-text:
Going to Sea
The sea has weather of its own. Wind rises and falls, storms cross the water and waves break on the shore.
Every vessel can crack, flood or sink, each in its own way. A raft that crosses a calm lake will not cross an ocean in a gale.

Before a crossing
- Watch the sky and the trees: a storm shows itself before it arrives. See Wind, Storms and Currents.
- Choose a vessel that suits the trip, and look at its hull for cracks. See Vessels and Their Repair.
- Take a bowl or a bucket to bail with, and the material that mends your vessel. See Surf, Swamping and Bailing.
- Decide where you will leave the vessel and how you will hold it there. See Mooring and Anchoring.

World settings
Choose the Rough Seas playstyle on the new world screen for a world with more open ocean.
Each mechanic of the sea has its own world setting under Rough Seas, all on by default: Water in the bilge, Hull damage, Lightning, Mooring strain, Currents, Rower fatigue and Pole's depth. Turn one off to leave it out of your game. Wind and storms come and go either way.
Turning Hull damage off mends every hull.
To change a setting in a world already made, use the /worldconfig command, then reload the world.
guide-weather-title: Rough Seas: Wind, Storms and Currents
guide-weather-text:
Wind
Wind has a direction and a strength, and it changes over hours.
The stronger the wind and the longer it blows over open water, the higher the waves. A big lake raises waves of its own.
Trees, clouds, rain and the roll of a boat all follow the wind. Look around before you push off to see how it blows.

Storms
Storms drift across the world, born where and when real ones are.
- Squalls are small. They come most in warm, wet summers and pass within hours.
- Gales sweep the middle latitudes and are strongest in winter. They cover a great area and blow for days.
- Hurricanes form over warm tropical seas from late summer into autumn. They last for days and bring the strongest wind of all.
A storm shows itself before it arrives: treetops start to sway, the sky darkens and the swell rises. Make for shore when you see it.

Lightning
Warm storms bring thunder, and lightning strikes inside them. Cold gales bring no thunder.
Keep a sailboat or an outrigger out of a thunderstorm: a mast draws lightning, and you sit at its foot.
A strike breaks up a light hull: a currach, a bark canoe, a raft or a coracle.

Currents
The oceans turn in great slow circles. The strongest current runs along an ocean's western shore, and small seas barely move.
In the middle latitudes that current carries warm water and the eastern side is cool. Nearer the equator and nearer the poles it is the other way round.
A vessel left alone drifts with the current. Tie it up or anchor it before you step ashore.
guide-vessels-title: Rough Seas: Vessels and Their Repair
guide-vessels-text:
Choosing a vessel
- Reed boat: two reed bundles bound with rope. Quick to build, low and wet, afloat a day at a time.
- Dugout: burnt and hewn out of five logs beside the water. The toughest hull on rivers and lakes, but it rolls in a sea.
- Coracle: a lattice of laths laid on the ground, bent up into a basket and covered with hides. It turns on the spot, and you carry it on your back.
- Bark canoe: a sheet of bark stripped off a standing birch, elm or spruce and framed where it lies. Fast and fragile, and it runs rapids.
- Hide currach: two long laths bound into a gunwale on the ground, framed upside down under hides and turned over. It carries cargo and rides over the swell.
- Outrigger canoe: a dugout rigged where it lies with a float, booms and a sail. Fast and steady on open sea.
- Sailboat: strong and roomy, the vessel for long voyages.
Each vessel's handbook page says how to build it.

Moving a vessel
Sit in the seat that steers, the tool in hand. walkforward and walkbackward drive the vessel, walkleft and walkright turn it.
- Hold a paddle to paddle in water of any depth.
- Hold a pole to push off the bottom. It reaches the bottom where the water is about a metre shallower than the pole is long. A crude oar is such a pole, two metres long.
- Row a currach with an empty hand: it has two oars of its own on thole pins.
A long, narrow hull runs fast, and a round or broad one goes slowly. A load slows any vessel.
Paddling, poling and rowing make you hungry.

Condition
Every vessel has a hull, and a knock cracks it where it lands: the bow, a side, a quarter or the bottom.
Look at a vessel to read each cracked place, from scratched through cracked and split to stove in. You also read how many litres a minute it leaks, and its freeboard, the height of its side above the water.
You see each crack on the hull where it is.
A vessel keeps its condition when you pick it up and place it again.

What cracks a hull
- Running into rock, the shore or another vessel at speed. The more aboard, the harder the knock: riders, cargo and above all water in the bilge. Ease in to a landing, and the hull takes no harm.
- Rapids, which batter the bottom of every hull except the bark canoe and the coracle.
- Breaking surf, lightning, explosions and weapons.
What a hull is made of decides how much it takes: a knock that cracks a bark canoe barely scratches a sailboat.
Build a dugout or an outrigger from hard wood, because the harder the wood, the tougher the hull. Any tree works, other mods' trees too.
Wood barely wears, so a wooden hull needs no upkeep.

Leaks
A crack in the bottom always leaks. A crack in the side leaks once a load sets the vessel low.
Leaks fill the bilge until the vessel swamps, and enough cracks outpace any bailing. See Surf, Swamping and Bailing.
Only a really severe blow breaks a hull up at once, or one that stoves in its last sound place.

Rafts, reed and hide
- A raft has no hull to fill, so knocks loosen its lashings instead. Once they are all loose, the raft comes apart into logs and rope.
- A reed boat's bundles give under knocks and take no harm. Reed soaks up water, though: after a day afloat the rider sits awash, and within four days the boat lies on the bottom. Lay it ashore in the sun to dry it out. It rots a little each time.
- A hide cover seeps at its seams. Grease it with rendered fat every few days to stop that. Untanned hide also rots afloat in warm water within days, so dry the boat ashore. Look at the boat to see when it needs either.
- An outrigger's float stands out to one side, so knocks from that side loosen the float's lashings rather than cracking the hull. Bind them up with flax twine before they give out, or the float and the rig come away and leave a plain dugout.

Mending
Hold the vessel's own material on its hull and keep rightmouse pressed. Each patch takes a while, and goes in once you have held it long enough.
The patch goes on the place you look at, or on the worst crack if that place is sound.
Each patch is hard work and makes you hungry. A hull with nothing left to mend says so.
Flax twine binds up a raft's lashings, and planks of the same wood mend a sailboat. Each boat's handbook page says what mends it.
A reed boat can't be mended. A broken vessel is gone: only floating wreckage is left.
guide-surf-title: Rough Seas: Surf, Swamping and Bailing
guide-surf-text:
Surf
A wave breaks where the water is too shallow for its height. In rough weather the last stretch to a beach is all surf.
A breaking wave strikes the side of the vessel it hits and can crack the hull there.
On a steep beach most waves plunge, and a plunging crest strikes far harder: it can stave in a hide boat.
Land in calm weather or in a sheltered bay, where the waves stay low.
Out at sea a wave breaks now and then too, more often the stronger the wind.

Water aboard
A wave higher than the vessel's side comes over it, and a crack lets water in from below.
A boat with a hull keeps that water in its bilge. A raft or a reed boat keeps none: the water washes through it.
Look at the vessel to read how many litres are in its bilge, how many litres a minute it leaks, and its freeboard, the height of its side above the water. You also see the water in the boat itself.
Water in the bilge weighs the boat down: it sits lower, ships more water, rolls harder and goes slower. Riders and cargo weigh it down the same way.
With no freeboard left, the sea comes over the side and floods the boat, cracked or not.

Swamping
A full bilge swamps the boat. You can't paddle a swamped boat or sit in it.
A light boat floats awash when swamped. A heavy one sinks: a sailboat with its ballast, a hull of a wood heavier than water, or a boat loaded heavy.
Hold on to a boat awash, bail it out once the sea calms, or swim away from it.
A sunk boat lies on the bottom with its cargo. Dive down to take the cargo out, or break the boat up with an axe for its wreckage.
A raft never swamps and holds its rider up even pressed under. A reed boat soaks up water until it sinks.

Bailing
Hold an empty bowl, jug or bucket.
Look into the boat, from beside it or seated in it, and hold rightmouse. Each scoop throws water over the side.
Look at the sea instead, and you fill the bowl from the sea.
A bucket bails fastest and keeps up with one bad leak. Several leaks outpace any bailing, so mend the cracks.
In a storm keep bailing, because every wave brings more water aboard. Don't leave a boat alone at sea in a storm: nobody bails it, and it swamps.
guide-mooring-text:
A vessel left alone drifts with the current, and a storm can throw it onto the shore. Tie it up or anchor it before you leave it.

Tying up
Tie a vessel to a fence post ashore with a rope, the way you tie an animal. Any vessel can be tied up.
The post holds the vessel, but a strong enough pull snaps the rope. The bigger the vessel, the harder the waves and the wind pull on it.
Pull a small boat ashore, or pick it up, before a gale.

Anchoring
A sailboat carries a stone anchor in its prow. Only the sailboat anchors.
rightmouse click the anchor with an empty hand to let it go, and again to haul it up.
The anchor lets out about five times the depth of the water in rope, and holds best that way. Its own rope reaches 120 metres.
For deeper water, stow an anchor warp at the foot of the mast with ctrl + rightmouse. It adds 90 metres.
- With too little rope out, the anchor drags in a storm.
- In water deeper than the rope, the anchor hangs and holds nothing.
- A rope that snaps takes the anchor with it.
While someone steers the boat, the anchor does not hold it but drags along behind.

Leaving a vessel
An anchored vessel takes the waves more gently, but it still ships water.
Near the shore with nobody around, a storm may throw a moored vessel up on the beach. Anchor it well out to keep it off the beach, and leave nothing that matters aboard.
